🐟CountershadingDark above, light belowAdaptationDeception

Countershading is camouflage through body coloration. Many open-ocean animals, including tuna and sharks, have darker backs and paler undersides.

  • Viewed from above: the dark back blends with the darker water below.
  • Viewed from below: the pale belly blends with brighter surface waters.

This can make an animal harder for predators or prey to spot. It reduces contrast; it does not make the animal invisible.

Try it with visitors

Look for a fish with a dark back and a light belly. Ask: “If you were looking up at this fish, what background would you see behind it?” Then ask how the background changes when looking down.

Compare with counter-illumination

Countershading uses body coloration. Counter-illumination uses light-producing structures on an animal’s underside to match light from above. The Bioluminescence section explains that related camouflage strategy.

Sources: Monterey Bay Aquarium — Open ocean; Smithsonian Ocean — Fish Using Counterillumination. External references require a connection; this explanation is available offline.
